title: Low-dose aspirin as primary prevention for adults without cardiovascular disease

sections.abstract: <jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Background:</jats:title> <jats:p>Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in the United States. Patients with cardiovascular disease risk factors are often put on low-dose aspirin to prevent future cardiovascular events and cardiovascular death. However, the evidence supporting this practice is limited.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Objective:</jats:title> <jats:p>To examine whether adults without a history of cardiovascular disease benefit from taking daily low-dose aspirin as primary prevention for cardiovascular disease and death.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Data sources:</jats:title> <jats:p>The four databases of PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, and Ovid were used, and a total of 67 nonduplicate articles were reviewed. After examining those articles, four studies were included. Of the four studies, three were randomized controlled trials, and one was a retrospective cohort study.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title> <jats:p>All four studies concluded that daily low-dose aspirin used for primary prevention does not lower the risk of death from cardiovascular disease.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Implications for practice:</jats:title> <jats:p>Further research needs to be conducted to determine whether daily low-dose aspirin is beneficial in individuals without a history of cardiovascular disease. Nurse practitioners need to know the most current evidence-based practice recommendations to appropriately counsel patients about whether they should be taking low-dose aspirin to prevent cardiovascular disease.</jats:p> </jats:sec>
